questions.stem: Evaluate 10!/8!.
questions.explanation: 10! = 10 × 9 × 8!, so 10!/8! = 10 × 9 = 90. Subtracting 8 from 10 to get 2 is not how factorials cancel, and 720 is 10 × 9 × 8.

questions.stem: Simplify (n + 1)!/(n − 1)!.
questions.explanation: (n + 1)! = (n + 1) × n × (n − 1)!, so the quotient is n(n + 1). Cancelling as if the factorials were ordinary numbers, (n + 1)/(n − 1), is a common error.

questions.stem: What is the value of 0! + 1!?
questions.explanation: By convention 0! = 1, so that n! = n × (n − 1)! also holds for n = 1. So 0! + 1! = 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.stem: A student has 4 shirts, 3 pairs of trousers and 2 pairs of shoes. How many different outfits of one of each are possible?
questions.explanation: By the multiplication principle, 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Adding, 4 + 3 + 2 = 9, counts single items rather than combined choices.

questions.stem: In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded to 3 of 8 runners?
questions.explanation: The medals are different, so order matters: P(8, 3) = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. The value 56 = C(8, 3) counts unordered groups of three, and 512 = 8³ allows one runner to win more than once.

questions.stem: Which formula gives P(n, r), the number of ordered selections of r objects from n distinct objects?
questions.explanation: P(n, r) = n(n − 1)...(n − r + 1), which is n!/(n − r)!. Dividing further by r! gives C(n, r), which ignores order.

questions.stem: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of BANANA?
questions.explanation: There are 6 letters with A repeated 3 times and N twice, so 6!/(3! × 2!) = 720/12 = 60. Dividing by 3! alone gives 120, which still counts swaps of the two Ns.

questions.stem: How many different arrangements are there of the letters of MISSISSIPPI?
questions.explanation: There are 11 letters: I four times, S four times and P twice, so 11!/(4! × 4! × 2!) = 34 650. Forgetting the repeated P gives 69 300.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a row if A and B must stand together?
questions.explanation: Treat A and B as one unit: 4 units in a row give 4! = 24 arrangements, and A and B can swap within the unit, so 2 × 24 = 48. Leaving out the swap gives 24.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a row if A and B must not stand together?
questions.explanation: All arrangements number 5! = 120, and 48 have A and B together, so 120 − 48 = 72. The value 48 counts the arrangements with them together.

questions.stem: How many arrangements of the letters of NUMBER begin and end with a consonant?
questions.explanation: The consonants are N, M, B and R. Choose the first and last in 4 × 3 = 12 ways, then arrange the other 4 letters in 4! = 24 ways: 12 × 24 = 288.

questions.stem: How many even four-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1 to 7 if no digit is repeated?
questions.explanation: Fill the restricted place first: the last digit is 2, 4 or 6 (3 ways), then the other places take 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ways, giving 360. The value 840 = P(7, 4) ignores the even condition.

questions.stem: How many four-digit numbers greater than 5000 can be formed from the digits 1 to 6 if no digit is repeated?
questions.explanation: The first digit must be 5 or 6 (2 ways), then the rest take 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ways, so 2 × 60 = 120. The value 360 = P(6, 4) counts every four-digit number.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 7 people be seated around a circular table?
questions.explanation: Around a circle, arrangements that are rotations of each other are the same, so there are (7 − 1)! = 6! = 720. The value 5040 = 7! counts arrangements in a row.

questions.stem: Why is the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in a circle (n − 1)!?
options: Each circular arrangement matches n rotations among the n! line orders
One object is left out of every circular arrangement
Clockwise and anticlockwise orders always count as the same
The first object in a circle can only go in one of n − 1 places
questions.explanation: Each circular arrangement corresponds to n different line arrangements, one starting from each person, so the count is n!/n = (n − 1)!. Reflections are not identified unless the problem says so, as with a necklace.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 8 people sit around a circular table if two particular people must sit together?
questions.explanation: Treat the pair as one unit: 7 units around a circle give 6! = 720 arrangements, and the pair can swap, so 2 × 720 = 1440. The value 10 080 = 2 × 7! treats the table as a row.

questions.stem: In how many ways can 7 people sit around a circular table if A and B must not sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: All arrangements number 6! = 720. With A and B together there are 2 × 5! = 240. So 720 − 240 = 480 have them apart.

questions.stem: Evaluate C(10, 3).
Which is equal to C(20, 17)?
questions.explanation: C(n, r) = C(n, n − r): choosing 17 to include is the same as choosing 3 to leave out. P(20, 3) is 3! times larger, since it counts order.

questions.stem: Choosing r objects from n distinct objects to include is matched by choosing which objects to exclude. Which identity does this prove?
questions.explanation: Each selection of r objects to include leaves exactly n − r to exclude, so the two counts are equal. The identity C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r) comes from splitting on whether one particular object is chosen.

questions.stem: Which is equal to C(9, 4) + C(9, 5)?
questions.explanation: Pascal's identity C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r), with n = 10 and r = 5, gives C(10, 5). Adding the top and bottom numbers to get C(18, 9) is not a valid rule.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 men and 2 women is chosen from 6 men and 5 women. How many committees are possible?
questions.explanation: Choose the men in C(6, 3) = 20 ways and the women in C(5, 2) = 10 ways, and multiply: 200. Adding 20 and 10 gives 30, and C(11, 5) = 462 ignores the requirement of 3 men and 2 women.

questions.stem: A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many committees include at least one woman?
questions.explanation: All committees number C(9, 4) = 126, and those with no women number C(5, 4) = 5, so 126 − 5 = 121. Choosing one woman first and then any 3 others, 4 × C(8, 3) = 224, counts many committees more than once.

questions.stem: If C(n, 2) = 45, what is n?
questions.explanation: C(n, 2) = n(n − 1)/2 = 45, so n(n − 1) = 90 = 10 × 9 and n = 10. Forgetting to divide by 2 leads to n(n − 1) = 45, which has no whole-number solution.

questions.stem: How many diagonals does a decagon (10 sides) have?
questions.explanation: Any 2 of the 10 vertices form a segment, giving C(10, 2) = 45, but 10 of those are sides, leaving 35 diagonals. The value 90 = P(10, 2) counts each segment twice.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red and 3 blue balls. In how many ways can 3 balls be chosen so that at least 2 are red?
questions.explanation: Split into cases: exactly 2 red, C(4, 2) × C(3, 1) = 18, plus exactly 3 red, C(4, 3) = 4, giving 22. Counting only the first case gives 18, and 35 = C(7, 3) counts every selection.

questions.stem: The letters A, B, C, D and E are arranged in a row at random. What is the probability that A is first and B is last?
questions.explanation: With A and B fixed, the other 3 letters can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways, out of 5! = 120 in all, so P = 6/120 = 1/20. Allowing A and B to swap ends gives 1/10.

questions.stem: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 5 boys and 4 girls. What is the probability that all three are girls?
questions.explanation: There are C(4, 3) = 4 all-girl committees out of C(9, 3) = 84, so P = 4/84 = 1/21. The value 64/729 = (4/9)³ treats the choices as made with replacement.

questions.stem: What are the coefficients in the expansion of (x + y)⁵?
questions.explanation: They are row 5 of Pascal's triangle, C(5, 0) to C(5, 5): 1, 5, 10, 10, 5, 1. There are six terms, one more than the power. The row 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 belongs to (x + y)⁴.

questions.stem: How many terms are in the expansion of (a + b)¹⁰?
questions.explanation: The powers of b run from 0 to 10, giving 11 terms. The number of terms is always one more than the power.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of x³y⁵ in the expansion of (x + y)⁸?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of x^(n − r)y^r is C(n, r), so here it is C(8, 5) = C(8, 3) = 56. The value 336 is P(8, 3), and 28 is C(8, 2).

questions.stem: Expand (2x − 1)⁴.
questions.explanation: Using 1, 4, 6, 4, 1: (2x)⁴ − 4(2x)³ + 6(2x)² − 4(2x) + 1 = 16x⁴ − 32x³ + 24x² − 8x + 1. The signs alternate because of the −1, and (−1)⁴ = +1 for the last term.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1 + 3x)⁵?
questions.explanation: The x² term is C(5, 2)(3x)² = 10 × 9x² = 90x². Forgetting to square the 3 gives 30.

questions.stem: What is the term in x² in the expansion of (x + 2)⁵?
questions.explanation: The x² term has x² and 2³: C(5, 3)x² × 2³ = 10 × 8x² = 80x². Pairing x² with 2² gives 40x², but the powers must add to 5.

questions.stem: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of (x + 2/x)⁶?
questions.explanation: The general term is C(6, k)x^(6 − k)(2/x)ᵏ = C(6, k)2ᵏx^(6 − 2k), which is constant when k = 3: 20 × 8 = 160. Leaving out the factor 2³ gives 20.

questions.stem: What is the term independent of x in the expansion of (2x − 1/x²)¹²?
questions.explanation: The general term is C(12, k)(2x)^(12 − k)(−1)ᵏx^(−2k), with power 12 − 3k, so k = 4. The term is C(12, 4) × 2⁸ × (−1)⁴ = 495 × 256 = 126 720, positive because the power of −1 is even.

questions.stem: What is the value of C(8, 0) + C(8, 1) + C(8, 2) + ... + C(8, 8)?
questions.explanation: Substituting x = 1 into (1 + x)⁸ = C(8, 0) + C(8, 1)x + ... + C(8, 8)x⁸ gives 2⁸ = 256. Equivalently, it counts all subsets of a set of 8 objects.

questions.stem: Substituting which value of x into the expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ shows that C(n, 0) − C(n, 1) + C(n, 2) − ... + (−1)ⁿC(n, n) = 0?
questions.explanation: With x = −1 the left side is (1 − 1)ⁿ = 0 and the right side alternates in sign. Substituting x = 1 gives the sum of the coefficients, 2ⁿ.

questions.stem: By comparing coefficients of x⁴ in (1 + x)⁴(1 + x)⁹ = (1 + x)¹³, the sum C(4, 0)C(9, 4) + C(4, 1)C(9, 3) + C(4, 2)C(9, 2) + C(4, 3)C(9, 1) + C(4, 4)C(9, 0) equals:
questions.explanation: Each product picks an x^k term from (1 + x)⁴ and an x^(4 − k) term from (1 + x)⁹, so together they give the x⁴ coefficient of (1 + x)¹³, which is C(13, 4). It also counts committees of 4 from 4 men and 9 women.

questions.stem: What is the value of C(5, 0)² + C(5, 1)² + C(5, 2)² + C(5, 3)² + C(5, 4)² + C(5, 5)²?
questions.explanation: Since C(5, k) = C(5, 5 − k), the sum is Σ C(5, k)C(5, 5 − k), the x⁵ coefficient of (1 + x)⁵(1 + x)⁵ = (1 + x)¹⁰. That is C(10, 5) = 252. The value 32 = 2⁵ is the plain sum of the coefficients.
